<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on the timing of Vedic rituals, specifically transitioning from the general rules of lunar days (tithis) to the specific observances of the month of Shravana, including the sacred thread renewal (Upakarma) and the festival of Raksha Bandhan.</meta>

### Ritual Timings and the Month of Shravana

Whether the ritual offerings should be performed on the earlier day or when there is a partial contact with the required time is a matter of debate; however, **Hemadri** <note>Hemadri Pant, a 13th-century scholar and author of the influential legal digest *Chaturvarga Chintamani*</note> argues for the earlier day. In the *Nirnaya-amrita* <note>a treatise on ritual timings</note>, it is decided that for the followers of the **Yajur Veda** <term>Yajur-shakhina</term> <note>practitioners of one of the four primary Vedas, focusing on sacrificial formulas</note>, the ritual of the herbs <note>part of the Upakarma ceremony</note> should be performed on the following day. 

In the *Rama-koshtaka* <note>an astrological or ritual manual</note>, the preference for the earlier day's pervasion is explicitly stated. Regarding new **Brahmacharis** <note>a student of Vedic knowledge who has undergone the Upanayana initiation</note>, the initiation into the study is mentioned here, though not its completion. Shaving the head is prescribed as a duty for these students and others authorized to perform the ritual.

The **Full Moon of Shravana** <term>Shravani Purnamasi</term> <note>the full moon day of the lunar month Shravana, marking the height of the monsoon</note> is the time for the ritual of **Pavitrarpana** <note>the offering of "pavitra" or consecrated silk/cotton threads to the deity</note>; this is a family duty that must be performed despite any minor ritual defects. On this day, the ceremonial oil bath is mandatory. On this same day, provided it is free from the influence of **Bhadra** <note>an inauspicious astrological period during which certain rituals are avoided</note>, the ritual of **Raksha Bandhan** <note>the "bond of protection," where protective threads are tied around the wrist</note> must be performed. For the **Shravana** ritual <note>the Upakarma</note>, it should be performed at sunset for those to be initiated. If the lunar day is partial, it may be performed during the remainder of the period.

<column-break/>

### The Festivals of Ganesha and Shitala

The annual **Sankata Chaturthi** <note>the "Fourth Day of Crisis," a fast dedicated to removing obstacles</note> is known as the day of the **Appearance of Ganesha**. This day should be observed when the fourth lunar day pervades the time of moonrise. If moonrise occurs during that lunar day on two consecutive days, the former day is chosen. 

However, **Madhava** <note>Madhavacharya, the 14th-century scholar and influential commentator</note> states that if the lunar day pervades the time when the ritual actually begins, the later day should be accepted. Regarding the third and fourth lunar days, they are preferred when they pervade the appropriate time; if they pervade both days, the former is chosen. 

For the **Shitala Vrata** <note>a ritual dedicated to Goddess Shitala, the "Cool One," to ward off smallpox and fevers</note> on the seventh lunar day, the earlier day should be taken. For the eighth lunar day <note>Ashtami</note> of the dark fortnight of **Shravana**, the day that pervades midnight should be accepted.

<summary>This page details the specific timing rules for the Shravana Upakarma, Raksha Bandhan, and Ganesha's appearance day, citing legal authorities like Hemadri and Madhava to resolve disputes over lunar days.</summary>

Cold distension and fullness in the heart and abdomen. It downbears qi and aids digestion. Eat it seasoned with sauce and vinegar.

<meta>catchword: And therefore</meta>

Among them are those who are compassionate, making a place for the Divine Presence <note>original: *Shekhinah*</note> to dwell among them, having received it from ancient days. This refers to the acceptance of the Torah. For "Who is this?" <note>Song of Songs 3:6</note> implies that while all the other nations refused to accept it, Israel did. This is a great merit that draws the Divine Presence down to the lower worlds. This is as the Sages taught in *Midrash Rabbah* on the verse, "And let them take for Me an offering" <note>Exodus 25:2</note>, using the parable of a king who had an only daughter, and so on. This means the "bed" <note>a metaphor for the place of union with God</note> exists because the acceptance of the Torah causes the Divine Presence to dwell. 

This is the secret of "Who is this... coming up from the wilderness?" <note>Song of Songs 3:6</note> It asks: what is the cause of her elevation and ascent from the wilderness? It is because of the "wilderness"—namely, the reception of the Torah there, as is explained. If so, the worthiness of their merit is clear, reaching unto the heavens. This is the secret of the phrase "like pillars of smoke"; by this power, they are worthy of this high level. Furthermore, she possesses the "merit of the ancestors" <note>term: *Zechut Avot* — the spiritual credit inherited from the righteousness of the Patriarchs</note>, a great and strong center that gives power and strength to the "branches" of the tribe. 

This is the secret of "perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all the powders of the merchant." As our Sages of blessed memory interpreted: 
"Myrrh" refers to our father Abraham; just as myrrh is the head of all spices, so was our father Abraham the head of all the righteous. 
"Frankincense" refers to our father Isaac, who was offered up like a handful of frankincense upon the altar. 
"All the powders of the merchant" refers to our father Jacob, whose "bed was complete" <note>original: *mitato shelemah*; a traditional idiom meaning all of his children were righteous and none were rejected</note>, and no defect <unclear>like this</unclear> was found in them. For they are compassionate in all matters of holiness, and it is fitting that you should take pity on the body of Jerusalem, that you should receive the Divine Presence, about which I have adjured you.

It is also possible that "perfumed with myrrh and frankincense" refers to the parts of the Torah. The Written Torah contains two parts: positive commandments and negative commandments. The negative commandments are likened to "myrrh" <note>original: *mor*</note>, as the Sages said that anyone who harvests it finds their hands are embittered; so too a person is embittered and finds it difficult to turn away from the pleasure of sins and their indulgence. Regarding the positive commandments, he says "frankincense," for they are sweet, heartening to the soul, and supportive of it. And regarding the Oral Torah, which consists of the words of the seeker and the wise, he says "and from all the powders of the merchant."

---

### Behold the bed of Solomon; sixty warriors are around it, of the warriors of Israel. <note>Song of Songs 3:7</note>

He also mentioned a great preparation for this attachment: the place where the Divine Presence dwells in the lower realms. This ensures that the ministering angels will have no cause to complain. He calls it "the bed of Solomon," meaning the Holy Temple <note>original: *Beit HaMikdash*</note>. He calls it a "bed" because just as a bed is designated for the union of husband and wife, so the Temple is designated to maintain the union of the Holy One, Blessed be He, with the Assembly of Israel here below. It is fitting that this "bed" be made with perfect intention, directed toward the dwelling place of the Name, may He be blessed, and the dwelling of His strength. 

It is also written that "sixty warriors" surround it. This refers to all the priestly watches, all the Levite watches, and the twelve divisions of Israel. As they said in the Midrash, they are all righteous and "warriors" in their ability to conquer their internal desires <note>term: *Yetzer Hara* — the "evil inclination" or base impulse</note>. This is the meaning of "warriors of Israel." Their merit is sufficient to sustain the matter and to guard Israel, even if the community as a whole lacks merit. All of this is an argument against the angels—that God's submission to dwell below is not purely an act of unearned grace, for there indeed exists the merit of these individuals, and these merits cause the fulfillment of His word, as we have said.

---

### They all hold swords, expert in war; every man has his sword upon his thigh, because of fear in the night. <note>Song of Songs 3:8</note>

He explained the strength of the aforementioned "warriors": they are warriors against their own desires. They are always standing armed on guard so that the inclination does not overcome them and cause them to stumble, even slightly...

It emphasizes that Israel's merit comes from accepting the Torah and overcoming internal moral struggles.</summary>

Indeed, according to Otto <note>original: Otho</note>, there was no question that could not be satisfactorily settled in this manner. For example, in 963, Otto was involved in a bitter exchange of accusations with Pope John XII—a conflict that preceded the Saxon emperors' eventual domination of the papacy. When Otto sent Bishop Liutprand to Rome to reject certain accusations made against him, he ordered his ambassador's armed attendants to defend his claims through a duel. The Pope, though he was himself skilled in using weapons, promptly declined this proposal.¹

In fact, a professional duelist seems to have been considered a necessary part of diplomatic missions. In 968, when Otto sent the same Liutprand to Constantinople to arrange a marriage, a dispute arose during the negotiations for the hand of Princess Theophania. The debate concerned the circumstances of Otto's conquest of Italy. The warlike bishop offered to prove his truthfulness through the sword of one of his attendants—an offer that brought the argument to a sudden and triumphant end.²

This willingness to leave the most important interests to the outcome of a judicial duel was not limited to Germany and Lombardy.
